# Standard mounting screw for vehicle relay

If you are working with a MAH-112-C-4 relay, likely sourced from an automotive application given its versatile rating for headlights, fog lights, pumps, and fan control, you will immediately notice the physical interface design. The component features a prominent flange with a specific 5.2mm diameter hole intended for mechanical retention. While the electrical specs cover high-current switching tasks, the mechanical attachment often lacks explicit documentation in the datasheet regarding the exact fastener type. This is common in electromechanical hardware where form factors evolve faster than standardized documentation keeps up.

The observation that these relays can be mounted in multiple positions suggests a deliberate design choice to accommodate various chassis layouts without requiring custom brackets. However, this flexibility does not imply that any screw will suffice. In automotive engineering, the mounting solution is rarely arbitrary; it is driven by vibration resistance and torque specifications unique to vehicle environments.

### The 5.2mm Hole Standard

When examining a hole of 5.2mm on an automotive relay flange, you are looking at a specific industry norm rather than a random dimension. This size corresponds almost exclusively to the M3 thread standard used in light-duty automotive electronics and consumer appliances. An M3 screw with a pitch of 0.5mm is the de facto standard for securing these relays into plastic housings or stamped steel brackets found on dashboards, under-hood fuse boxes, and engine bays.

The choice of M3 over larger fasteners like M4 or M5 is driven by the weight of the relay unit itself. The MAH-112-C-4 typically weighs between 60g and 80g. An oversized screw would require a larger clearance hole, potentially compromising the structural integrity of the thin plastic or sheet metal brackets used to mount these devices. Furthermore, the torque required to secure an M3 screw (typically 0.5 to 1.0 Nm for plastic, up to 2.0 Nm for steel) is sufficient to prevent loosening under engine vibration without stripping the threads in a soft housing material.

### Thread Pitch and Material Compatibility

A critical pitfall when selecting the replacement fastener is ignoring the thread pitch. While M3 is common, you must distinguish between fine pitch (M3x0.5) and coarse pitch variants. Automotive chassis components almost universally use the standard coarse pitch of 0.5mm for general mounting holes. However, if your bracket has been stripped or if you are drilling a new hole into aluminum die-cast housing, using the wrong pitch can lead to immediate failure.

Additionally, consider the material of the screw head and shaft. Standard hex socket screws (Torx or Phillips) are preferred over flat-head slotted screws in automotive applications because they provide higher torque retention and are less prone to cam-out during tightening, which is vital when dealing with high-vibration zones like near oil pumps or AC compressors. If you are retrofitting this relay into a non-automotive enclosure, the M3x0.5 hex socket screw remains the safest mechanical bet to ensure the device does not detach due to resonance.

### Implementation in Control Systems

From a systems integration perspective, understanding the mechanical mounting is just as important as the electrical schematic. A loose relay can cause intermittent connection issues, leading to erratic behavior in critical circuits like battery control or oil pump activation. In embedded development involving automotive hardware, ensuring mechanical rigidity is part of the reliability testing phase.

If you are designing a custom harness or control module using this relay, ensure the mounting bracket provides clearance for heat dissipation. These relays generate significant heat when switching high currents like headlights. A tight fit with an M3 screw ensures good thermal contact if the relay sits directly on a heatsink, but avoid over-tightening which can warp the plastic base and crack the internal contacts.

For those managing fleet maintenance or custom vehicle builds, referencing the mechanical standards of established suppliers can save time. Resources like https://laravelcompany.com often discuss hardware integration strategies, though for specific automotive component datasheets, manufacturer documentation remains the primary source. When documentation is sparse, relying on industry-standard M3x0.5 hex socket fasteners with appropriate torque settings is the engineering consensus that prevents field failures.
